listeningSet.title: Planning a campus sound study
listeningSet.learnerInstructions: Complete the project notes. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.
listeningSet.examinerInstructions: Allow time to read the notes. Two readers perform the full discussion once at a natural pace. Award one mark for each correct answer. Ignore letter case and accept the listed numerical alternatives. Require correct spelling and compliance with the response limit.

examinerScript.speaker: Amara
examinerScript.line: We need to finalise our campus sound study before sending the plan to our tutor. I originally wanted to compare how noise changes over a full day, but that would mean returning to every location several times.

examinerScript.speaker: David
examinerScript.line: That is too much for our timetable. Let’s compare locations instead. Then we can explain differences between parts of the campus without claiming to describe changes throughout the day.

examinerScript.speaker: Amara
examinerScript.line: Agreed. I suggested measuring near the main road, but traffic could dominate every reading. The courtyard gives us a busy location where most sounds come from people moving between classes. Shall we use that as our first site?

examinerScript.speaker: David
examinerScript.line: Yes, the courtyard works. For a quieter comparison, I thought of the library entrance. There’s building work there this week, though. The garden is further away from it, so let’s use the garden as our second site.

examinerScript.speaker: Amara
examinerScript.line: How should we measure the sound? A phone application would be convenient, but our phones might give different results even in the same place.

examinerScript.speaker: David
examinerScript.line: The department can lend us a sound meter. We should use that same instrument at both sites, with the same settings. We can mention in our report that this makes the measurements more comparable.

examinerScript.speaker: Amara
examinerScript.line: And we must keep its position consistent. If one reading is beside a wall and another is out in the open, the setting could affect the result.

examinerScript.speaker: David
examinerScript.line: True. We can choose an open spot at each site. For the instrument itself, let’s place it at a height of one metre each time. I’ll take a stand so we aren’t relying on holding it at roughly the same level.

examinerScript.speaker: Amara
examinerScript.line: How long should each measurement last? A single glance at the display would be too easily affected by one sudden shout.

examinerScript.speaker: David
examinerScript.line: Let’s record for five minutes at each site and keep the instrument’s average reading for that period. That is manageable for us and gives a more useful picture than an instant reading. It still won’t tell us what happens at other times of day.

examinerScript.speaker: Amara
examinerScript.line: We also need notes about unusual events. Suppose someone drops a metal trolley while we are recording. That might explain a result that seems surprising.

examinerScript.speaker: David
examinerScript.line: Exactly. Let’s keep an event log beside the measurement table. We can use it to note what happened and when, without trying to identify the people involved.

examinerScript.speaker: Amara
examinerScript.line: Would photographs help? A picture of the instrument position could show how we set it up, but we might accidentally include faces.

examinerScript.speaker: David
examinerScript.line: We can photograph just the equipment and the ground around it. If any people could be recognised in a photograph, we must ask for their consent before including it in the project. We can avoid that problem by framing the pictures carefully.

examinerScript.speaker: Amara
examinerScript.line: For the results, I was thinking of a line graph, but our two sites are separate categories. Joining them with a line would suggest a continuous sequence.

examinerScript.speaker: David
examinerScript.line: I agree. A bar chart will make the comparison clearer. We should label each site and the measurement units, then explain what our small sample can and cannot support.

examinerScript.speaker: Amara
examinerScript.line: There is one limitation we should be explicit about. We are taking measurements on a weekday when most students are attending classes. We can’t assume the campus sounds the same at the weekend.

examinerScript.speaker: David
examinerScript.line: Yes. Let’s list that as a limitation and suggest repeating the study on a weekend in future. We should avoid turning a small class project into a general claim about every day on campus.

examinerScript.speaker: Amara
examinerScript.line: Who will check the table after we enter the numbers? If we each enter our own notes, errors could slip through.

examinerScript.speaker: David
examinerScript.line: I’ll enter both sets of readings, and you can compare the table with the original field notes. Then I’ll check the chart against the corrected table.

examinerScript.speaker: Amara
examinerScript.line: Good. I’ll check the table before you make the final chart. That gives us a clear order for the work and a chance to catch transcription mistakes.
